Ask Jesus Into Your Heart
ask JEE-zus IN-too yor hart
phrase (imperative)
A revivalist invitation-formula popularized in nineteenth- and twentieth-century American evangelism, drawn loosely from a misread of Revelation 3:20 ('Behold, I stand at the door, and knock') and from a sentimental reading of 'Christ may dwell in your hearts by faith' (Eph. 3:17). The phrase makes the sinner's decisive act the inviting of Jesus inward, often sealed by a one-time prayer.

Biblical Verdict

🟠
Examine
A sentimental substitute for the biblical call to repent and believe; recover the real summons, honor the genuine desire to receive Christ.

Biblical Definition

Nowhere does Scripture command a sinner to 'ask Jesus into your heart.' The apostolic summons is sharper and clearer: 'Repent ye, and believe the gospel' (Mark 1:15); 'repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins' (Acts 2:38); 'believe on the Lord Jesus Christ, and thou shalt be saved' (Acts 16:31). Faith and repentance, not the recitation of an invitation, are the response the gospel demands. The verse the phrase leans on, Revelation 3:20, is addressed not to the unconverted but to a lukewarm church Christ calls to repentance; and Ephesians 3:17, that 'Christ may dwell in your hearts by faith,' is Paul's prayer for believers already saved, not a formula for sinners to perform. There is a real and precious truth buried under the cliche: Christ does come to dwell in the regenerate, and the heart is the seat where He is received. But He is received by repentant faith in His finished work, not summoned in by a decision the sinner manufactures.

Era

A sentimental revival-formula with no command behind it; the biblical summons is 'repent ye, and believe the gospel' (Mark 1:15) — recover the real call, while honoring the genuine desire to receive Christ.

ASK JESUS INTO YOUR HEART, phrase. A revivalist invitation to receive Christ by inviting Him inward, often by a one-time prayer.

Texts misapplied: Rev. 3:20 (addressed to a lukewarm church, not the lost) and Eph. 3:17 (a prayer for believers).

The biblical response: repentance and faith — 'repent, and believe' (Mark 1:15); 'believe on the Lord Jesus Christ' (Acts 16:31); 'repent, and be baptized' (Acts 2:38).

The genuine kernel: Christ truly indwells the regenerate (Gal. 2:20) — but He is received by faith in His finished work, not summoned by a manufactured decision.

Key Scripture

Mark 1:15 — "And saying, The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand: repent ye, and believe the gospel."

Acts 16:31 — "And they said, Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ, and thou shalt be saved, and thy house."

Acts 2:38 — "Then Peter said unto them, Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost."

Revelation 3:20 — "Behold, I stand at the door, and knock: if any man hear my voice, and open the door, I will come in to him, and will sup with him, and he with me."

John 1:12-13 — "But as many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of God, even to them that believe on his name: Which were born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God."

Ephesians 3:17 — "That Christ may dwell in your hearts by faith; that ye, being rooted and grounded in love,"

Modern Corruption

A sentimental formula displaces the biblical summons — 'repent and believe' becomes 'ask Jesus in,' a one-time decision that can leave a sinner assured by a prayer he prayed rather than by Christ whom he trusts.

expand to see more

The corruption is not malice but drift: a real desire — to receive Christ — channeled into a formula Scripture never gives, with real costs. The gospel's command is 'repent ye, and believe' (Mark 1:15), a turning from sin and a resting of the whole soul on Christ crucified and risen. 'Ask Jesus into your heart' quietly substitutes a single inward invitation, often a prayer repeated after a leader, and then treats the praying of that prayer as the saving act. The man is taught to look back to a decision he made and a sentence he spoke, rather than forward and upward to the Christ he is to trust. Many who 'asked Jesus in' as children, with no repentance and no continuing faith, were given a false assurance built on a transaction rather than on the Savior.

The texts cannot bear the weight laid on them. Revelation 3:20 is Christ's word to the lukewarm church of Laodicea, a call to a backslidden congregation to repent and renew communion, not an altar-call to the unconverted. Ephesians 3:17 is the apostle's prayer that believers — already 'rooted and grounded in love' — would know Christ's indwelling more deeply. To make either verse the proof-text for a sinner's inviting Jesus inward is to misread both. And John 1:12-13 guards the door the cliche leaves open: those who receive Him are born 'not of the will of man, but of God' — receiving Christ is the fruit of the new birth God works, not a decision the natural man generates to trigger it.

The recovery is to preach the real summons and let the kernel stand. There is a true and glorious sense in which Christ comes to dwell in His people: 'Christ liveth in me' (Gal. 2:20), 'Christ in you, the hope of glory' (Col. 1:27). The honest longing behind the cliche — to belong to Christ, to have Him near — is good and is answered. But the way to that indwelling is not a formula; it is to repent and believe, casting oneself wholly on the Lord Jesus Christ. Call sinners not to invite Jesus in as a guest they admit, but to flee to Him as the Savior who alone can make them new.

Hebrew Roots

A revival-formula with no biblical command behind it; Scripture says 'repent and believe' (Mark 1:15). Christ truly indwells the regenerate, but He is received by repentant faith, not summoned by a one-time prayer.

English: a nineteenth/twentieth-century American revivalist invitation, drawn loosely from a misread of Rev. 3:20 and Eph. 3:17.

The real summons: Mark 1:15 ('repent ye, and believe the gospel'); Acts 16:31 ('believe on the Lord Jesus Christ').

The genuine kernel: Gal. 2:20 / Col. 1:27 — Christ truly dwells in His people; the longing the cliche voices is answered by faith, not formula.

Usage

"He had 'asked Jesus into his heart' at seven and never once repented; the prayer he remembered had become a pillow over an unconverted soul."

"Christ told the lukewarm church to open the door (Rev. 3:20); He told sinners to repent and believe (Mark 1:15) — and we have swapped the two."

"Do not invite Christ in as a guest you admit; flee to Him as the Savior who alone makes the dead alive."
